beats.narration: Chapter 30 is the biggest thing I have taken on in this project. It carries 1,654 sentences, more than five times Chapter 25. Fifty-five of them were flagged for verification, and those 55 assertions spread across 111 evidence rows, because one sentence can lean on several sources. Thirty-five fell inside my scope, plus 6 editorial findings.

beats.narration: Of the 35 assertions I reviewed, 24 need revision and 11 are approved as written. One number matters more than the split. Every single row the earlier verification pass had already marked false turned out to be a genuine error. Eleven out of eleven. Not one of them was a false alarm, which is the opposite of what I found in Chapter 25.

beats.narration: The clearest error in the chapter is two numbers in the wrong places. The textbook says a screen of 15 compounds identified 10 anticancer agents. The study actually screened a library of 2,427 drugs and found 15 hits, of which 10 were anticancer agents. The 15 is the number of hits, not the number screened. That understates the work by two orders of magnitude and makes the hit rate meaningless.

beats.narration: This one I liked, because we found where it came from. The chapter names Mycoplasma hominis as the bacterium whose enzyme inactivates gemcitabine. The documented species is Mycoplasma hyorhinis. Then I opened a 2021 review, and its body text says hyorhinis while a figure caption in the same paper says hominis. The wrong name is already loose in the published literature. The chapter probably inherited it rather than inventing it.

beats.narration: I ran four full checks on my own work, and every one of them found something. The second caught my own document truncating links at 46 characters and shipping four broken ones. The third found newer evidence, a 2026 five-year update I had missed. The fourth caught three sources cited on rows they did not actually support, and one of my own corrections quietly introducing a new problem.

beats.narration: Three findings I could not verify are reported as unverified rather than wrong, because that distinction is the honest one. And the practical blocker is not a content error at all. The workbook recorded character encoding damage in four files. It is actually in seven, including eight broken arrows nobody had logged. That has to be repaired and committed before any text edit, or find and replace fails silently.

beats.narration: So here is what I would hand to you. Take any report that cites its sources. For each citation, do not just check that the link opens. Check that the source actually speaks to the claim it is attached to. A real paper sitting on the wrong row is still a broken citation.
